chunks.title: Sahkarmi
chunks.text: Sahkarmi: Open-source desktop platform where AI coworkers do real operational work on your own machine, with human approval before anything consequential. Status: Released · Microsoft Store · Scoop. Period: Oct 2026 – present. Stack: Electron 43, TypeScript, SolidJS, Claude Agent SDK, Model Context Protocol, Codex app-server, ACP, Vitest, GitHub Actions. Repository: https://github.com/ganguydhrubo/sahakarmi. Live at https://sahkarmi.site. Sahkarmi is a Windows desktop application in which configurable AI coworkers browse, file, draft and report inside sandboxed browsers and local tools. It is built on the Apache-2.0 OpenBot v0.1.11 base and extended by more than 110,000 lines: a multi-provider agent runtime, a 16-category permission policy with non-overridable gates, Telegram remote approvals, offline voice, 175 coworker templates and a release pipeline that ships checksums, an SBOM and provenance attestations.

chunks.title: Sahkarmi
chunks.text: Sahkarmi problem: Small businesses want agents that act, not chat. The risk is an agent that pays, posts, deletes or submits something nobody authorised. Sahkarmi's design rule is simple: the model proposes, a human approves, and the decision is recorded.

chunks.title: Sahkarmi
chunks.text: Sahkarmi architecture: Agent runtime: Claude Agent SDK with canUseTool gating, OpenAI Codex app-server, and an Agent Client Protocol (ACP) bridge to OpenCode and Gemini runtimes, all behind one coworker abstraction. Tools: in-process MCP servers for browser, files and integrations; user-configurable MCP servers (stdio or HTTP, up to 30); Composio app connectors. Approval architecture: 16 permission categories; payments, customer messages, publication, shell access, deletions and official forms always ask; time-boxed delegated authority; a browser take-over flow so agents never handle passwords or OTPs. Remote control: Telegram bridge for approvals and status with per-chat allow-lists. Electron hardening: context isolation, sandbox, strict CSP, Electron fuses, 209 sender-validated IPC channels. Release engineering: CI on every PR, tag-driven release with SHA-256 checksums, SPDX SBOM, GitHub build-provenance attestation and electron-updater.

chunks.title: Sahkarmi
chunks.text: Sahkarmi evidence: Releases: 69 published (v0.3.0 to v0.33.0); History: 498 commits, 103 merged PRs; Distribution: Microsoft Store, Scoop bucket; Tests: About 650 Vitest cases (counted 2 Nov 2026); Diff over base: +110,740 / -3,142 lines, 438 new files; Store ID: 9PD6BP3NGVST; Locales: 12.

chunks.id: project:sahkarmi:decision:Why approval gates are not overridable
chunks.title: Sahkarmi
chunks.section: Why approval gates are not overridable
chunks.text: Sahkarmi. Why approval gates are not overridable. A policy that an agent can talk its way around is not a policy. The six highest-impact categories are hard-coded to ask; the model cannot auto-approve them, and the UI cannot be configured to skip them.

chunks.title: Sahkarmi
chunks.section: Why build on OpenBot instead of from scratch
chunks.text: Sahkarmi. Why build on OpenBot instead of from scratch. OpenBot provided a working Electron shell and Codex client under Apache-2.0. Starting there bought weeks; the attribution is kept in NOTICE and the diff is public.

chunks.title: Sahkarmi
chunks.text: Sahkarmi. Why local-first. The target users keep customer data on their own machines and do not have an IT team. Sandboxed per-coworker browsers and local storage keep the blast radius small.

chunks.title: Sahkarmi
chunks.text: Sahkarmi limitations and honest status: Windows only; the installer is not yet code-signed, so SmartScreen warns on first run. Single maintainer; roughly half of the commits were co-authored with Claude Code and are reviewed, tested and released by one person. Labelled a development preview; adoption numbers are small and are not quoted here.

chunks.title: Who is Dhrubojyoti Gangopadhyay?
chunks.text: Who is Dhrubojyoti Gangopadhyay? Dhrubojyoti Gangopadhyay, known as Dhrubo, is a forward deployed and applied AI engineer based in Kolkata, India. He builds agentic systems that connect language models to the tools, data and approval steps a business already runs on. Before engineering he spent sixteen years (2007 to 2023) in enterprise revenue operations at AGM level in cement and steel distribution. He is the builder of Sahkarmi, an open-source desktop AI-coworker platform, and currently works as a Forward Deployed AI Engineer at 1XL Universe.

chunks.title: What does Dhrubo build?
chunks.text: What does Dhrubo build? Agentic systems for business operations: desktop AI coworkers with human approval gates (Sahkarmi), multi-tenant SaaS with messaging and payment integrations (AuraLeads, Zappy), an AI website builder with a Cloudflare publishing pipeline (ATITTLE), and a set of public LangGraph and RAG prototypes in Python. Everything is open source and listed with its real status on the projects page.

chunks.title: What is Sahkarmi and how is it built?
chunks.text: What is Sahkarmi and how is it built? Sahkarmi is a Windows desktop application in which configurable AI coworkers browse, file, draft and report on the user's own machine, with every consequential action stopped for human approval. It is built with Electron, TypeScript and SolidJS on an Apache-2.0 OpenBot base, uses the Claude Agent SDK, the OpenAI Codex app-server and an Agent Client Protocol bridge, exposes tools over the Model Context Protocol, and ships with a 16-category permission policy, Telegram remote approvals, offline voice and 175 coworker templates. It has 69 published releases, about 650 unit tests, and is listed on the Microsoft Store and a Scoop bucket.

chunks.title: What is a forward deployed AI engineer?
chunks.text: What is a forward deployed AI engineer? A forward deployed AI engineer works directly with the people who have a business problem, scopes a workflow a language model can improve, builds and deploys it into the tools those people already use, and stays until the metric moves. The role combines discovery and scoping with hands-on engineering and change management, as opposed to pure research or pure solutions engineering.

chunks.title: How does an enterprise operations background connect to AI engineering?
chunks.text: How does an enterprise operations background connect to AI engineering? Operations is where automation meets consequences. Sixteen years of dealer networks, rebate systems and reconciliation taught Dhrubo that plausible output from a trusted system is the most dangerous kind of wrong. That instinct shapes how he builds agent systems: structural approval gates, structured execution records instead of chat transcripts, and evaluation sets before deployment.

chunks.title: Which technologies does Dhrubo work with?
chunks.text: Which technologies does Dhrubo work with? TypeScript, Node.js, Electron, SolidJS, React and Next.js; Python and FastAPI; the Claude Agent SDK, Model Context Protocol, LangGraph, hybrid retrieval (BM25 plus vector) with Chroma or pgvector; PostgreSQL and Supabase with row-level security; Redis Streams; Cloudflare Workers and KV; Vercel; Docker; GitHub Actions; Vitest, pytest and Playwright. Model providers used in shipped code include Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible APIs (Groq, OpenRouter, Cerebras), Google Gemini and local models.

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do. The permission model behind Sahkarmi: sixteen action categories, six that can never be auto-approved, time-boxed delegated authority, and a browser take-over flow that keeps passwords away from the model. Published 2026-11-02. Topics: human-in-the-loop, AI agent permissions, approval workflow, MCP, Claude Agent SDK.

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: Most agent demos answer one question well: what did the model say? Operations work asks a harder one: what did the system actually do, and who allowed it? Sahkarmi is a desktop platform where AI coworkers browse, file, draft and report on a user's own Windows machine. This article is about the part of it I spent the most design time on, which is the part that stops the agent. The failure we are designing against An agent with a browser and a shell can pay an invoice, message a customer, submit a government form, publish a page or delete a folder. Each of those is a one-way door. A chat assistant that hallucinates wastes a minute; an agent that hallucinates a bank transfer costs real money and trust. So the first design rule in Sahkarmi is blunt: The model proposes. A human approves. The decision is recorded.

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: Everything below is machinery to make that rule cheap enough that people keep it switched on. Sixteen categories, six hard gates Every tool call an agent can make is classified into one of sixteen permission categories in permission-policy.ts : reading files, writing files, browsing, form filling, payments, external messages, publication, shell access, deletions, official forms, and so on. Each category has a default decision: allow, ask, or deny.

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: Six categories are special. Payments, messages to customers or third parties, publication, shell commands, destructive file operations and official or government forms are hard-coded to ask . The model cannot auto-approve them. The settings UI cannot switch them to allow. A coworker template cannot override them. The reasoning is simple: a policy an agent can talk its way around is not a policy, and a setting a tired user can flip at midnight is not a safeguard. Delegated authority with an expiry

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: Asking on every action makes an agent useless for repetitive work, so Sahkarmi has an approval store with two kinds of memory. A specific approval ("yes, send this message") is single-use. A delegated approval ("you may send order confirmations to existing customers for the next thirty days") is scoped to a category and a pattern and carries a hard expiry. Nothing is remembered forever; the store evicts delegated authority at thirty days and plain approvals at seven. Expiry is not a UX nicety. It forces the user to re-read what they have delegated. The browser take-over flow

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: The most common place an agent meets a secret is a login page. The naive design is to give the agent the password. Sahkarmi refuses. When a coworker reaches a login or a one-time code, it requests secure input. The sandboxed browser is handed to the human, who signs in with their own hands; the coworker then takes the session back. The model never sees the password or the OTP, which means it can never log them, leak them into a transcript or be tricked into typing them somewhere else. Each coworker gets its own browser profile, so a coworker that handles supplier portals never shares cookies with the one that drafts marketing posts. Approvals from your phone

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: Operations do not wait for someone to be at a desk. The Telegram bridge forwards approval requests to an allow-listed chat and accepts a decision back. The bridge is deliberately narrow: it can approve, reject and report status, and nothing else. A compromised phone can let a pending action through; it cannot start new work. What this looks like in code

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: The agent runtime is the Claude Agent SDK, and the hook is canUseTool . Every tool call is routed through the permission policy before execution; the policy returns allow, deny or a pending-approval token. The same policy guards the Codex app-server path and the Agent Client Protocol bridge to OpenCode and Gemini runtimes, so switching models does not change what the system is allowed to do. Tools arrive over the Model Context Protocol, including user-configured MCP servers, which means third-party tools inherit the same gates as built-in ones.

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: A short honesty note: the gates are enforced in the Sahkarmi host, not in the model. For non-Claude runtimes that call tools through their own loop, the policy is applied at the tool boundary the bridge controls. If a runtime had a side channel the bridge does not mediate, the policy would not see it. That is why the Electron shell is hardened separately: context isolation, sandbox, a strict CSP, Electron fuses and sender-validated IPC on all 209 channels. Costs This design has prices. Approval fatigue is real; the fix is good defaults in the 175 coworker templates, so the ask prompts are rare and specific. Delegation expiry annoys power users. The take-over flow adds a minute to any task that needs a login. I think every one of these is worth paying, because the alternative is an agent whose worst day is unbounded. What I would do next

chunks.title: Approval gates for AI agents: how Sahkarmi decides what a coworker may do
chunks.text: Three things are missing. Approval requests should show a diff of the effect, not a description of the intent. Delegations should be exportable so an owner can audit what their staff have granted. And the policy needs a formal test suite that proves no path from any runtime can reach a gated category without a token. The test files exist for the policy itself; the end-to-end proof across runtimes does not yet. Sahkarmi's source, releases and permission policy are public on GitHub. The project page on this site lists what is verified and what is not: Sahkarmi.

chunks.title: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does
chunks.text: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does. Not a solutions engineer, not a researcher. A working definition of the forward deployed AI engineer role, drawn from doing it inside a company and from reading a hundred job descriptions. Published 2026-11-02. Topics: forward deployed engineer, FDE, applied AI engineer, AI adoption.

chunks.title: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does
chunks.text: The title "forward deployed engineer" was popularised by Palantir and is now on job boards from Databricks to Sarvam. The AI version of the role is defined inconsistently. Having read about a hundred postings while preparing a job search, and having done the work inside a company since mid-2026, this is my working definition. The one-sentence version A forward deployed AI engineer sits with the people who have the problem, scopes a workflow a language model can improve, builds it, deploys it into the tools those people already use, and stays until the numbers move.

chunks.title: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does
chunks.text: Each clause rules something out. "Sits with the people" rules out building from a ticket. "Scopes a workflow" rules out building a chatbot and hoping. "Builds it" rules out pure solutions engineering. "Deploys into existing tools" rules out a demo on a laptop. "Stays until the numbers move" rules out handing over a repo and leaving. What the week looks like In my current role at 1XL I own AI adoption across HR, sales, marketing, operations, support, finance and technology. A typical week includes:

chunks.title: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does
chunks.text: - Discovery. Sitting with a department head and watching the work. Most "we need AI" requests turn out to be a data-entry problem, an approval-chain problem or a reporting problem. The model is sometimes the smallest part. - Scoping. Writing one page: the input, the output, who approves, what happens when the model is wrong, and the metric. If I cannot write the failure paragraph, the project is not ready. - Building. Usually a small service: a document goes in, structured data comes out, a human reviews, a system of record is updated. Python or TypeScript, a hosted model behind an adapter, a queue if volume needs it. - Teaching. Role-specific curricula and field manuals, because a tool nobody can operate is not deployed. The induction programme for new joiners in the India and UAE offices is part of this. - Infrastructure advice. Which messaging platform, which workflow engine, where the data may live. For us that has meant WhatsApp infrastructure, n8n and agentic-workflow tooling.

chunks.title: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does
chunks.text: What it is not It is not research. I do not train models and I do not claim to. It is not pure solutions engineering either; a solutions engineer demonstrates the product, a forward deployed engineer changes the customer's process and ships code into it. It is not an internal tools team: the measure of success is a departmental metric, not a shipped feature. The skills that matter, in order

chunks.title: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does
chunks.text: 1. Scoping judgement. Knowing which 20 percent of a process is worth automating and which 80 percent should be left to a human with a better form. 2. Integration plumbing. Auth, webhooks, idempotency, retries, logging. Most of the code in a forward deployed project is not AI. 3. Evaluation. A fixed test set, a judge, and a number that moves. Without it every demo is a success and every deployment is a surprise. 4. Guardrails. Approval steps before consequential actions. I wrote about how Sahkarmi does this in Approval gates for AI agents. 5. Explaining. To a finance head who will never read the code, in their vocabulary. Model knowledge is on the list, but it is fifth or sixth. Providers change monthly; scoping judgement does not. Why a revenue-operations background helps

chunks.title: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does
chunks.text: I spent sixteen years in enterprise revenue operations before writing software full time. That turns out to be the right preparation for the first two skills on the list. I have been the person whose approval chain was bypassed by a clever spreadsheet, and the person who had to reconcile what the system said against what the dealer received. Operations people can tell when an engineer has never been on the receiving end of their own automation. How to evaluate a candidate for this role If you are hiring, look for three artefacts. A deployed system with an approval or review step in it, not a demo. An evaluation set with a number attached. And a document written for a non-technical owner that explains what the system will not do. Résumés list frameworks; these three show judgement.

chunks.title: What a forward deployed AI engineer actually does
chunks.text: If you want to see mine, the projects page lists every public system with an honest status, and the résumé is one page.

chunks.title: Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion: notes from a RAG prototype
chunks.text: Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion: notes from a RAG prototype. Why dense and sparse retrieval disagree, why fusing ranks beats blending scores, and what a 20-question evaluation set revealed about a B2B sales-intelligence prototype. Published 2026-11-02. Topics: RAG, hybrid search, BM25, reciprocal rank fusion, re-ranking, RAG evaluation.

chunks.title: Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion: notes from a RAG prototype
chunks.text: This is a set of notes from a retrieval prototype, the B2B Sales Intelligence RAG repository. It is a prototype: it has fifty unit tests, a twenty-question evaluation set and no deployment. The notes are about the retrieval design, which is the part I would reuse. The problem with one retriever A sales team asks questions like "which accounts in the North East mentioned a budget freeze on a call in the last quarter?" The useful evidence lives in CRM notes, call transcripts and account plans. Two retrieval families fail in opposite ways on this: - Dense retrieval (embeddings) understands "budget freeze" and "spending pause" are the same thing. It is poor at exact tokens: account codes, product SKUs, a person's surname, a region string. - Sparse retrieval (BM25) nails exact tokens and dates and is blind to paraphrase.

chunks.title: Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion: notes from a RAG prototype
chunks.text: Sales questions always contain both kinds of signal. So the retriever uses both and then has to combine them. Why fuse ranks instead of scores The tempting approach is final = a dense score + b bm25 score . It does not work in practice because the two scores live on different scales and distributions, and the right a and b change with the corpus. You end up tuning a magic number per customer. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) avoids the scales entirely. Each retriever returns a ranked list; a document's fused score is the sum over retrievers of 1 / (k + rank) , with k typically 60. A document ranked first by both retrievers wins; a document ranked first by one and absent from the other still surfaces. The prototype applies a weight per retriever on top of that, which is the only knob, and in the evaluation it barely needed moving. Re-ranking the fused list

chunks.title: Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion: notes from a RAG prototype
chunks.text: RRF gives a good top fifty, not a good top five. A cross-encoder re-ranker reads the query and each candidate together and scores relevance directly. It is too slow to run over the whole corpus and exactly fast enough to run over fifty candidates. The prototype uses a small open cross-encoder; the quality jump from fused top-k to re-ranked top-k was the single largest improvement in the evaluation. The evaluation set Twenty questions is small, and it was still the most useful artefact in the project. Each question has an expected set of source documents and a reference answer. An LLM judge scores the generated answer for faithfulness to the retrieved context and for coverage of the reference. Retrieval is scored separately with recall at k, which is the number that actually told me whether a change helped.

chunks.title: Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion: notes from a RAG prototype
chunks.text: Three things the set revealed: 1. Chunk size mattered more than the embedding model. Transcripts needed smaller chunks with overlap; account plans needed whole sections. 2. BM25 alone beat dense alone on this corpus, because sales questions are full of proper nouns. Fusion beat both. 3. The judge was lenient on answers that hedged. Faithfulness scoring needs a strict rubric or it rewards vagueness. What is honest to say about this prototype The dependency pins did not resolve in CI, so the tests have never run in a pipeline, only locally. There is no deployment and no production traffic. I include it here because the retrieval and evaluation design is sound and reusable, and because the projects page exists to show status honestly rather than to impress. What I would do in production

chunks.title: Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion: notes from a RAG prototype
chunks.text: Trace every query with the retrieved IDs and scores so failures can be replayed. Grow the evaluation set from real questions, not invented ones. Add a freshness feature, because sales context goes stale in weeks. And keep RRF; in a year of reading about retrieval I have not found a simpler combiner that works as reliably.

chunks.title: Sixteen years of revenue operations taught me to distrust unaudited automation
chunks.text: Sixteen years of revenue operations taught me to distrust unaudited automation. Dealer rebates, reconciliation by hand and approval chains that broke silently: what cement and steel distribution teaches about building AI systems for operations. Published 2026-11-02. Topics: revenue operations, enterprise AI adoption, workflow automation, audit trail.

chunks.title: Sixteen years of revenue operations taught me to distrust unaudited automation
chunks.text: Between 2007 and 2023 I worked in revenue operations for building-materials and consumer companies: Johnson & Johnson, Ramco Cements, ACC, Lafarge, MP Birla Cement, Star Cement and Shyam Steel, finishing at AGM level. The last seven of those years were mostly about dealer rebate and incentive systems. That is where I learned the instincts I now use to build AI systems. Rebates are automation with money attached A cement dealer earns rebates on volume, on timely payment, on product mix and on quarterly targets. Each rule is a small program. Multiply by thousands of dealers and dozens of schemes, and the rebate system is the largest automated decision-maker in the company. It moves more money than any individual manager approves in a year.

chunks.title: Sixteen years of revenue operations taught me to distrust unaudited automation
chunks.text: At MP Birla I inherited a scheme calculation with structural errors: a slab boundary applied inconsistently, a mix bonus that double-counted one product family. Nobody had noticed because the output looked plausible and the system was trusted. Fixing it recovered leakage across the national network, and the lasting lesson was not about rebates. It was that plausible output from a trusted system is the most dangerous kind of wrong. Three failure patterns I keep seeing

chunks.title: Sixteen years of revenue operations taught me to distrust unaudited automation
chunks.text: The silent bypass. An approval chain exists on paper. A clever spreadsheet or a WhatsApp message to the right person routes around it. The audit trail shows a clean process that did not happen. In agent systems the equivalent is a model that finds a tool path the policy did not anticipate. The fix is the same in both worlds: make the gate structural, not procedural. That is why the highest-impact categories in Sahkarmi are hard-coded to ask and cannot be configured away.

chunks.title: Sixteen years of revenue operations taught me to distrust unaudited automation
chunks.text: Reconciliation by hand. At Star Cement and Shyam Steel, the gap between what the system said was shipped, invoiced and collected and what the distributor experienced was closed by people with printouts. Every month. Automation that does not produce a reconcilable record just moves the manual work downstream. In agent systems this means structured execution records, not chat transcripts. "The agent said it sent the email" is a transcript; "message ID, recipient, timestamp, approver" is a record. Delayed approvals that become default approvals. When the approver is slow, the organisation learns to proceed without them, and the approval becomes decorative. Agent systems have the same pressure: an approval prompt that fires too often gets clicked through. The answer is scoped, expiring delegation, so routine work flows and exceptions still stop. What this changes about how I build

chunks.title: Sixteen years of revenue operations taught me to distrust unaudited automation
chunks.text: I write the failure paragraph before the happy path. I design the record before the feature. I assume the first version of any rule has a structural error and I build the check that would catch it. I treat a demo that works as the beginning of the evaluation, not the end. And I am sceptical of my own automation in a way that only comes from having been on the receiving end. When a distributor in Guwahati calls because the scheme statement does not match their ledger, "the system calculated it" is not an answer. The same is true when an agent sends the wrong message to a customer. The bridge

chunks.title: Sixteen years of revenue operations taught me to distrust unaudited automation
chunks.text: People ask how sixteen years of commercial operations connect to writing agent systems. The connection is that operations is where automation meets consequences. Engineers who have not lived there tend to optimise for what the model can do. Operators optimise for what happens when it is wrong. A forward deployed AI engineer has to do both, and I think the second instinct is the rarer one. If you run operations and are considering agents, the work with me page describes how I scope these projects, and the approval gates article shows the design in code.
